q: 3-Methylbut-1-yne is treated separately with (I) H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, HgSO<sub>4</sub> and (II) 1. disiamylborane 2. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH. Which pair names the products correctly?
h: Decide Markovnikov vs anti-Markovnikov for each, then remember both reactions pass through an enol.
w: Mercury-catalyzed hydration is Markovnikov: OH on C2, then the enol tautomerizes to the methyl ketone, 3-methylbutan-2-one. A bulky dialkylborane puts boron on C1 (anti-Markovnikov); oxidation gives the enol HO–CH=CH–, which tautomerizes to the aldehyde, 3-methylbutanal.
x: The regiochemistry is reversed: HgSO<sub>4</sub> hydration is Markovnikov (ketone), hydroboration is anti-Markovnikov (aldehyde).
Hydroboration–oxidation of an alkyne gives an enol that tautomerizes to the aldehyde; an alcohol would need a reduction step.
Alkyne hydration gives an enol that tautomerizes to a ketone, not an alcohol.

q: Why is a bulky dialkylborane such as disiamylborane or 9-BBN used, instead of BH<sub>3</sub>, to hydroborate a terminal alkyne?
c: After one addition, the vinylborane still has a π bond; the bulky borane adds only once, so oxidation gives the aldehyde.
BH<sub>3</sub> adds with Markovnikov regiochemistry to alkynes, so it would give a ketone.
BH<sub>3</sub> cannot add to C≡C bonds; only dialkylboranes react with alkynes.
The bulky borane is needed to make the enol tautomerize to the aldehyde.
h: Think about what is left after the first B–H adds across the triple bond.
w: Hydroboration of a triple bond leaves a C=C (a vinylborane), which can react with a second B–H. A small borane like BH3 can add twice and has three B–H bonds that react further. The steric bulk of Sia2BH or 9-BBN stops the reaction after one addition (and reinforces boron on the terminal carbon), so H2O2/NaOH gives the enol and then the aldehyde.
x: BH<sub>3</sub> also adds boron to the less substituted carbon; the problem with BH<sub>3</sub> is double addition, not regiochemistry.
BH<sub>3</sub> does react with alkynes; it just does not stop cleanly after one addition.
Enol-to-aldehyde tautomerization occurs on its own under the basic oxidation conditions; the borane plays no part in it.

q: What is the major product of but-2-yne with one equivalent of Br2 in CH2Cl2?
h: Halogen addition to a π bond goes through a bridged bromonium ion. Which face does Br<sup>−</sup> attack, and how many equivalents add?
w: As with alkenes, Br2 adds to an alkyne mainly anti, so the two Br atoms end up on opposite sides of the new C=C. With one equivalent the product is the dibromoalkene (E)-2,3-dibromobut-2-ene.
x: The Z isomer would require syn addition; bromination is mainly anti.
The tetrabromide forms only with two (or more) equivalents of Br<sub>2</sub>.
A saturated vicinal dibromide would need an extra H<sub>2</sub>; Br<sub>2</sub> adds only Br atoms, leaving a C=C.

q: An alkyne C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>12</sub> is treated with 1. O<sub>3</sub> 2. H<sub>2</sub>O. The only products are propanoic acid and butanoic acid. Which alkyne was it?
h: Ozonolysis cuts the triple bond and turns each sp carbon into a COOH carbon. Rejoin the two acid carbons with a triple bond.
w: Ozonolysis of an internal alkyne breaks C≡C completely, giving two carboxylic acids (a terminal ≡CH becomes CO2). Joining the carboxyl carbons of CH3CH2COOH (C3) and CH3CH2CH2COOH (C4) gives CH3CH2C≡CCH2CH2CH3, hept-3-yne.
x: Hept-2-yne would give acetic acid (C2) and pentanoic acid (C5).
This alkyne would give propanoic acid and 2-methylpropanoic acid, a branched C4 acid, not butanoic acid.
A terminal alkyne gives one carboxylic acid (here hexanoic acid) plus CO<sub>2</sub>.

q: Compound X (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) takes up 2 equiv H<sub>2</sub> over Pt to give C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>. Treatment of X with 1. O<sub>3</sub> 2. H<sub>2</sub>O gives a single product, octanedioic acid, HOOC(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>6</sub>COOH. Which structure is X?
h: Count degrees of unsaturation and how many are π bonds. If the product keeps all 8 carbons with a COOH at each end, where was the cleaved bond?
w: C8H12 has 3 degrees of unsaturation; 2 equiv H2 removes two π bonds, so X has one ring plus a triple bond (or two C=C). Ozonolysis giving a single C8 diacid means one multiple bond was cut inside a ring, leaving both cut carbons as COOH groups on the same chain. Both new COOH carbons come from a triple bond (alkyne ozonolysis gives acids). That is cyclooctyne, the smallest isolable cycloalkyne.
x: Ethynylcyclohexane fits the formula and H<sub>2</sub> uptake, but ozonolysis gives cyclohexanecarboxylic acid and CO<sub>2</sub>, not an open-chain diacid.
Cycloocta-1,5-diene also fits the formula, but cutting both C=C bonds gives two C<sub>4</sub> fragments, not one C<sub>8</sub> product.
Cleaving both C=C bonds of 1-vinylcyclohexene gives a C<sub>7</sub> fragment and a one-carbon fragment, not a single C<sub>8</sub> diacid.

q: Which sequence, starting from acetylene (HC≡CH), gives hexanal?
h: Count carbons: acetylene brings 2. Then decide which hydration puts the C=O on the terminal carbon.
w: Hexanal, CH3(CH2)4CHO, has 6 carbons with the carbonyl at C1. Acetylene (2 C) + a butyl group (4 C) gives hex-1-yne. Anti-Markovnikov hydration with the bulky borane then gives the aldehyde: 1. NaNH2 2. butyl bromide 3. Sia2BH 4. H2O2, NaOH.
x: HgSO<sub>4</sub> hydration of hex-1-yne is Markovnikov and gives hexan-2-one, not hexanal.
Hydroxide is too weak a base to make the acetylide (water, pKa 15.7, is far more acidic than acetylene, 25).
A pentyl halide gives hept-1-yne, so the final aldehyde is heptanal (7 C), one carbon too many.

q: Which sequence converts acetylene into the alkene shown?
h: Build the full carbon skeleton as an alkyne first (two alkylations), then choose the reduction that sets the alkene geometry.
w: The target is (E)-oct-4-ene: two propyl groups on a trans C=C. Alkylate acetylene twice with 1-bromopropane (deprotonate before each alkylation) to make oct-4-yne, then reduce with Na, NH3(l), which gives the trans (E) alkene.
x: Lindlar hydrogenation is syn and gives (Z)-oct-4-ene, the wrong stereoisomer.
Reducing too early turns the terminal alkyne into an alkene, which has no acidic C–H for NaNH<sub>2</sub>, so the second alkylation fails.
Isopropyl bromide is secondary; acetylides do E2 with it (propene forms), and even S<sub>N</sub>2 would give a branched skeleton.

q: Which route is best for preparing the ketone shown as a single product?
c: HC≡CH; 1. NaNH<sub>2</sub>  2. (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br  3. H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst  4. H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
h: A methyl ketone comes cleanly from Markovnikov hydration of a terminal alkyne. What happens when an unsymmetrical internal alkyne is hydrated?
w: The target is 5-methylhexan-2-one, CH3CO–CH2CH2CH(CH3)2. Alkylating acetylide with the primary halide 1-bromo-3-methylbutane gives the terminal alkyne 5-methylhex-1-yne; HgSO4 hydration is Markovnikov and gives only the methyl ketone. So the best route is HC≡CH; NaNH2; (CH3)2CHCH2CH2Br; HgSO4/H2SO4/H2O.
x: This makes the internal alkyne 5-methylhex-2-yne; hydration of an unsymmetrical internal alkyne gives a mixture of the 2-one and the 3-one.
Hydroboration–oxidation of the terminal alkyne gives the aldehyde, 5-methylhexanal, not the methyl ketone.
Acid-catalyzed hydration of the alkene gives an alcohol (5-methylhexan-2-ol), not a ketone.

q: Which reagent converts hept-1-yne into heptane?
h: Which reducing conditions do not stop at the alkene stage?
w: An active metal catalyst (Pd/C or Pt) with excess H2 adds two equivalents of H2 and does not stop at the alkene: hept-1-yne → heptane. The other conditions either stop at the alkene or do not reduce C≡C.
x: Lindlar's poisoned catalyst stops after one H<sub>2</sub>, giving hept-1-ene.
Dissolving-metal reduction stops at the alkene (and a terminal alkyne is largely deprotonated under these conditions).
NaBH<sub>4</sub> delivers hydride to polar C=O bonds; it does not reduce nonpolar C≡C bonds.

q: Which statement correctly describes the reduction of an internal alkyne by Na in NH<sub>3</sub>(l)?
c: Electrons are added one at a time; the vinyl radical and vinyl anion intermediates prefer the trans geometry before NH3 protonates them.
Hydrogen atoms are delivered to one face from the surface of the sodium metal, so the product is trans.
NH<sub>3</sub> first protonates the alkyne to give a vinyl cation, which Na then reduces.
The cis alkene forms first and then isomerizes to the more stable trans alkene in NH3.
h: The sequence is electron, proton, electron, proton. Which intermediate decides the geometry?
w: Na donates an electron to give a radical anion; NH3 protonates it to a vinyl radical, which adopts the less crowded trans arrangement; a second electron gives a vinyl anion that keeps the trans geometry and is protonated by NH3. The trans product therefore comes from the preferred geometry of these intermediates.
x: Na is not a hydrogenation surface; it supplies electrons, and the H atoms come from NH<sub>3</sub>. (Surface delivery would be syn and give cis.)
NH<sub>3</sub> is far too weak an acid to protonate an alkyne; the first step is electron transfer from Na.
No cis alkene forms; the geometry is set in the vinyl radical/anion stage, and simple alkenes do not isomerize under these conditions.

q: Acid-catalyzed hydration of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene gives a methyl-shift product. What is the final product when 3,3-dimethylbut-1-yne is treated with H2O, H2SO4, HgSO4?
h: Mercury-catalyzed alkyne hydration does not go through a free carbocation. Where does OH go, and what does the enol become?
w: Hg2+ activates the triple bond without forming a free carbocation, so no methyl shift occurs. Water adds Markovnikov (OH on C2), and the enol tautomerizes to the ketone: 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-one.
x: The aldehyde is the anti-Markovnikov product, obtained by hydroboration–oxidation, not by HgSO<sub>4</sub> hydration.
This rearranged alcohol is what the alkene gives through a free carbocation; the alkyne hydration gives a ketone with no rearrangement.
This enol is the first-formed intermediate; under the acidic conditions it tautomerizes to the ketone.

q: Which compounds give 2,2-dichlorobutane as the major product with excess HCl?
h: HCl adds Markovnikov. In a vinyl chloride, a cation next to Cl is stabilized by the Cl lone pair.
w: I (but-1-yne): two Markovnikov additions put both Cl on C2 → 2,2-dichlorobutane. II (but-2-yne): the first HCl gives 2-chlorobut-2-ene; the second protonates C3 so the cation sits on the Cl-bearing C2 → 2,2-dichlorobutane (C2 and C3 are equivalent at the start). III is that same vinyl chloride: protonation at C3 gives the Cl-stabilized cation at C2, and Cl− adds there. So I, II, and III all give 2,2-dichlorobutane.
x: III is a vinyl chloride; HCl adds so the cation forms on the Cl-bearing carbon, giving the same geminal 2,2-dichloride.
The symmetric internal alkyne II also gives the geminal dichloride at C2 (equivalent to C3), so I alone is incomplete.
Terminal alkyne I adds HCl Markovnikov twice, putting both Cl on C2, so it must be included.

q: What is the major product when pent-1-yne reacts with one equivalent of HCl?
h: Markovnikov: H goes to the carbon that already has more H atoms. How many HCl add?
w: H+ adds to terminal C1 so the vinyl cation forms on C2 (the more substituted sp carbon). Cl− adds to C2, giving the vinyl halide 2-chloropent-1-ene. Only one equivalent adds, so the product keeps a C=C.
x: Cl on C1 is the anti-Markovnikov product; HCl does not add anti-Markovnikov, even with peroxides.
The double bond stays between C1 and C2; HCl addition does not move it to C2–C3.
The geminal dichloride needs a second equivalent of HCl.

q: Sodium acetylide is to be alkylated with 1-bromopropane. Which solvent must not be used?
h: Compare the acidity of each solvent with that of acetylene (pKa ≈ 25).
w: Acetylide is the conjugate base of an acid with pKa ≈ 25. Ethanol (pKa ≈ 16) is a much stronger acid, so it protonates the acetylide immediately (Keq ≈ 109) and destroys the nucleophile. NH3 (38), THF and ether are far weaker acids and are suitable.
x: NH3 (pKa 38) is a weaker acid than acetylene, so it does not protonate acetylide; it is the usual solvent for these reactions.
THF has no O–H and its C–H bonds are far less acidic than acetylene, so it is a suitable aprotic solvent.
Diethyl ether is aprotic and does not protonate acetylide ions.

q: Pent-4-yn-1-ol is treated with 2 equiv NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then 1 equiv CH<sub>3</sub>I, then H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the major product?
h: Two equivalents remove both the most acidic H (O–H, pKa ≈ 16) and the next (≡C–H, ≈ 25). Which anion of the dianion is the stronger base and nucleophile?
w: NaNH2 first removes the O–H proton, then the terminal ≡C–H, giving a dianion. The acetylide carbanion (conjugate acid pKa 25) is a much stronger base and better nucleophile than the alkoxide (conjugate acid pKa 16), so the one equivalent of CH3I alkylates carbon. Water then protonates the alkoxide: hex-4-yn-1-ol.
x: Alkylation at oxygen would require the alkoxide to outcompete the more reactive acetylide; the more basic anion of a dianion reacts first.
Only 1 equiv of CH<sub>3</sub>I is present, and the alkoxide is the less reactive site, so dimethylation is not the major outcome.
The propargylic CH2 is not deprotonated by NaNH2 (pKa well above 38), so no carbanion forms there.

c: 1. H<sub>2</sub>, Lindlar catalyst  2. BH<sub>3</sub>·THF  3. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH
h: Hydroboration of an alkyne stops at a carbonyl compound. To reach a primary alcohol in one oxidation step, what must the hydroboration substrate be?
w: Partial hydrogenation (Lindlar) gives hex-1-ene; hydroboration–oxidation of the alkene is anti-Markovnikov and gives the primary alcohol hexan-1-ol. Hydroborating the alkyne directly gives an enol that becomes hexanal, which would still need a reduction.
x: Hydroboration–oxidation of the alkyne gives hexanal (via the enol), an aldehyde rather than the alcohol.
Acid-catalyzed hydration of hex-1-ene is Markovnikov and gives hexan-2-ol.
HgSO<sub>4</sub> hydration gives hexan-2-one, and NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces it to the secondary alcohol hexan-2-ol.

q: Alkyne X (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) gives the same single ketone with either H<sub>2</sub>O/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/HgSO<sub>4</sub> or 1. Sia<sub>2</sub>BH 2. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, NaOH. Ozonolysis of X (1. O<sub>3</sub> 2. H<sub>2</sub>O) gives one carboxylic acid and no CO<sub>2</sub>. Which structure is X?
h: A terminal alkyne gives different products with the two hydration methods and loses its ≡CH carbon as CO<sub>2</sub> on ozonolysis. What internal alkyne gives one product from each?
w: Getting the same single ketone from Markovnikov and anti-Markovnikov hydration requires the two sp carbons to be equivalent, and a single acid with no CO2 on ozonolysis also requires an internal, symmetric alkyne. Hex-3-yne gives hexan-3-one by both methods and two molecules of propanoic acid on ozonolysis.
x: Hex-1-yne gives hexan-2-one with HgSO<sub>4</sub> but hexanal with Sia<sub>2</sub>BH, and its ozonolysis releases CO<sub>2</sub>.
Hex-2-yne is unsymmetric: each hydration gives a mixture of hexan-2-one and hexan-3-one, and ozonolysis gives two different acids (acetic and butanoic).
This terminal alkyne gives a methyl ketone with HgSO<sub>4</sub> but an aldehyde with Sia<sub>2</sub>BH, and ozonolysis gives CO<sub>2</sub>.
